## From five separate labs to one platform

Every architecture diagram you've seen this week showed one slice of the
system in isolation. In production none of those slices run alone — a
lakehouse with nothing feeding it is empty, a vector index with nothing
governing its source data is a liability, and a quality gate that nobody
wired into the pipeline is just a notebook cell. Enterprises that build AI
platforms combine all of it into a single ecosystem that can, at scale:

- Collect data
- Process data
- Store data
- Govern data
- Retrieve knowledge
- Power AI applications
- Deliver real-time intelligence

That list is the whole week, restated as one pipeline. The rest of this page
is that pipeline made concrete.

## The reference architecture

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A["Data Sources<br>APIs · IoT · ERP · CRM · Files"] --> B
    B["Real-Time Data Pipelines<br>Kafka / Spark / Flink / Airflow"] --> C
    C["Data Quality &amp; Validation Layer"] --> D
    D["Governance &amp; Security Layer<br>Access · Policies · Compliance"] --> E
    E["Modern Data Architecture<br>Lakehouse / Warehouse / Mesh"] --> F
    F["Embedding &amp; Vectorization Layer"] --> G
    G["Vector Database<br>ChromaDB / Pinecone / Weaviate"] --> H
    H["Advanced RAG System<br>Retrieval + Re-ranking + LLMs"] --> I
    I["AI Applications &amp; Agents"]
```

Every box in that diagram is something you already built this week:

| Layer | What it is | Where you built it |
|---|---|---|
| Real-Time Data Pipelines | Streaming ingestion with schema validation at the door | Day 2 |
| Data Quality & Validation | Automated checks before bad data reaches production | Day 4 |
| Governance & Security | Access policies, compliance, lineage tracking | Day 4 |
| Modern Data Architecture | Bronze/Silver/Gold lakehouse with ACID guarantees | Day 1 |
| Embedding & Vectorization / Vector DB | Chunking, embeddings, similarity search | Day 3 |
| Advanced RAG System | Retrieval + reranking + LLM response generation | Day 3 |

The architectural insight isn't any single box — it's the **order and the
gating**. Data quality sits *before* governance, and governance sits *before*
storage, because a system that governs or stores bad data has already failed;
catching it earlier is strictly cheaper. RAG serving sits at the very end,
downstream of everything else, because a RAG answer is only as trustworthy as
the governed, quality-checked data it was indexed from — this is the direct,
practical answer to Day 3's question of why RAG systems hallucinate: they
retrieve from whatever they were given, so if the retrieval corpus was never
quality-gated, the model will confidently ground its answer in garbage.

## How the components work together, step by step

Walking the diagram top to bottom as a single request's journey:

**Step 1 — Data ingestion.** Real-time pipelines collect events from APIs,
IoT devices, operational databases (via CDC), documents, and other
enterprise systems, and land them on a topic — this is Day 2's Kafka
producer/consumer model.

**Step 2 — Data quality validation.** Automated checks validate schema
correctness, missing fields, duplicate records, and invalid values before
anything is allowed further downstream. Bad data is blocked here, not
discovered later in a dashboard — this is Day 4's quality gate.

**Step 3 — Governance enforcement.** Governance systems apply access
policies, enforce security boundaries, track lineage, and monitor
compliance. This is also Day 4, and it's why lineage exists: a governance
rule with no lineage trail can't tell you what a policy change will actually
affect.

**Step 4 — Data storage.** Validated, governed data lands in the lakehouse —
bronze (raw), silver (cleansed), gold (aggregated) — using the Delta Lake
ACID guarantees, `MERGE`, and schema enforcement from Day 1.

**Step 5 — Embedding generation.** Documents and records are converted into
vector embeddings using an embedding model (Day 3's sentence-transformers or
equivalent).

**Step 6 — Vector storage.** Those embeddings are persisted in a vector
database (Chroma, Pinecone, Weaviate) for similarity search.

**Step 7 — RAG retrieval.** AI systems retrieve the relevant enterprise
knowledge semantically, rather than relying on keyword search alone.

**Step 8 — AI response generation.** An LLM generates a response grounded in
the retrieved context — the payoff of every layer beneath it having done its
job correctly.

## Recommended technology stack

The slide deck's stack-by-layer table is a reasonable default if you're
choosing tools for a real deployment (not everything on it is required for
this course's capstone — see [The Final Project](02_final_project.qmd) for
what's actually graded):

| Layer | Recommended technologies |
|---|---|
| Data Pipelines | Kafka, Spark, Flink |
| Storage | Databricks, Snowflake (or open Delta Lake / Iceberg on cloud object storage) |
| Quality | Great Expectations |
| Governance | Collibra, Purview |
| Embeddings | Sentence Transformers |
| Vector DB | Pinecone, ChromaDB |
| RAG | LangChain, LlamaIndex |
| LLMs | GPT, Qwen, Claude |

## Orchestrating the platform

None of the layers above wire themselves together. **AI infrastructure
orchestration** is the automated coordination of compute, storage,
networking, and AI services so the pipeline above runs reliably, efficiently,
and at scale — the conductor making sure ingestion, quality gating, storage,
embedding, and serving each run at the right time without stepping on each
other.

### Workflow orchestration: the DAG

The tool most directly relevant to this week's labs is **Apache Airflow**,
which models a pipeline as a **DAG** (Directed Acyclic Graph) — tasks as
nodes, dependencies as edges, executed in topological order:

- **Operators** are the task types: `PythonOperator`, `BashOperator`,
  `SparkSubmitOperator`, `S3KeySensor`, `HttpSensor`.
- **Key configuration:** `schedule_interval` (cron expression), `start_date`,
  `retries`, `retry_delay`, `catchup=False` (don't backfill every missed run
  since `start_date`).
- **XCom** is a lightweight key-value store for passing data *between* tasks
  — keep it small (row counts, file paths, IDs), never whole DataFrames.
- **`BranchPythonOperator`** returns the `task_id` to run next, enabling
  conditional pipeline paths — exactly the "if quality gate fails, quarantine
  instead of serving" branch the capstone's Module 5 already models.
- **Best practice:** one DAG per pipeline, idempotent tasks (safe to re-run
  without duplicating side effects), and a sensor for every external
  dependency instead of a fixed sleep/wait.

### Beyond workflows: the other orchestration layers

At real enterprise scale, "orchestration" splits into more than just DAG
scheduling. This is background context for how the tools you used this week
get operated in production — not something the capstone requires you to
stand up:

| Orchestration layer | Manages | Example tools |
|---|---|---|
| Compute | GPU/CPU allocation across workloads | Kubernetes, Kueue, Volcano, Karpenter |
| Workflow | Multi-step pipeline dependencies | Airflow, Prefect, Dagster, Temporal |
| Model | Embedding models, rerankers, LLMs in production | vLLM, Triton, BentoML, Ray Serve |
| Vector DB | Index rebuilds, shard rebalancing, backups | Coordinated with the data lake's own backup schedule |
| Data | Movement and quality across pipeline stages | Kafka, dbt, Great Expectations, dlt |

Without this coordination, the failure modes are concrete: a GPU training job
starves a vector DB of latency budget, an embedding job starts before its
upstream chunks are ready, scaling requires slow manual provisioning, one
pipeline failure takes down the whole system instead of retrying in
isolation, and a version upgrade breaks consumers mid-pipeline instead of
rolling out as a canary. Orchestration exists specifically to turn each of
those into an automated, recoverable non-event.

## Why integration is the point

A fully integrated platform is what moves an enterprise from an AI prototype
to production: real-time streaming, governance compliance, automated data
validation, and semantic RAG search working as one system instead of four
disconnected demos. That combination is what delivers **fast, safe, and
reliable** AI applications at scale — better AI accuracy because the RAG
layer only ever sees governed, quality-checked data; fewer hallucinations
because responses are grounded in a trusted corpus, not whatever happened to
be lying around; and governance and compliance enforced automatically instead
of depending on someone remembering a policy.

The [final project](02_final_project.qmd) is where you build exactly this,
end to end, for a real (if intentionally small) dataset.
